extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mass communication/media studies; journalists and media policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the external forces (advertisers, governments, markets, military, technology) that shape media content and the formal/informal standards, regulations, and practices that mediate that influence. Used for coursework, research, or policy analysis in media studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-created programming (purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program-length content conceived originally as a vehicle to provide product exposure to the child audience (or other audiences), in the hopes of stimulating product sales and sustaining program popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such programming is not sold for entertainment value first; it is designed primarily to promote merchandise. Example: JC Penney producing a decorating video that includes merchandise prices; Macy's proposed cable channel devoted to selling store merchandise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer creative control over advertiser-created programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative control for the program content is typically relinquished to the manufacturer of the product upon which the program is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers specify how characters must look, what they can or cannot say or do, and what environments they live in—i.e., the advertiser/producer dictates editorial and creative choices rather than broadcasters or independent producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated advertising: commercials intertwined with content
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming is being developed with commercials so skillfully intertwined with other information that they cannot be removed or avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertiser-created programs and videocassettes/discs/cable channels may embed advertising within content to prevent viewers from erasing or skipping messages (Janus, 1984). This blurs distinction between editorial content and promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infomercial format and distribution (30-minute advertising productions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-form commercials (infomercials) of about 30 minutes used to pitch products, including celebrity endorsements and customer testimonials, with orders taken by toll-free numbers and credit cards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since ~1988 infomercials grew substantially (over $750 million in 1994). They often use low-key but effective sales tactics; examples include celebrity-led pitches (Victoria Jackson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising crossing into editorial/news coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising material can be produced or staged in ways that lead news media to cover it as news/editorial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political or promotional pieces can be run to generate free news exposure (Roger Ailes on news media using ads as news leads). This criterion flags when promotional materials are treated as legitimate news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government controls mechanism (laws, regulations, licenses, taxes, financing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments exert control over mass media through formal tools: laws, regulations, licenses, taxes; and in state-owned systems, through financing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In privately owned media systems, controls operate via legal/regulatory levers; in government-owned systems control is exerted via funding decisions (Janus, 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: State censorship and repression tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of methods governments use to repress or control journalists and media: banning publications, forbidding journalists to write or sign their articles, restricting travel or passports, arrests, kidnappings, physical attacks, death threats, assassinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom House data example: press-freedom violations (kidnappings, arrests, assaults, killings). Specific examples: Algeria forbidding journalists to write/sign/ travel; South Africa's stringent censorship; wartime or emergency censorship like Russia in 1993.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government monopoly/ownership of media as control
rubrics_metrics.description: When the state owns media outlets (newspapers, TV, radio), it can make editorial decisions directly and impose unwritten rules on portrayal and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Doordarshan in India run by government with politicians making editorial decisions; PRC ownership leading to rules like 'portray even negative things in a positive light' and promotion of lightweight/sensational content as press forced to support itself financially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal provisions enabling censorship or bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory or code provisions that permit banning or restriction of material (e.g., banning books or periodicals of foreign origin) as a tool to harass or control dissenting media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: French press code provision used to ban émigré magazine El-Badil multiple times (1986–1989). Such formal provisions provide legal cover for restricting certain publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-ordered disclosure of sources (limiting reporter protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial rulings that compel journalists to reveal their sources (e.g., when faced with defamation suits), reducing confidentiality protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Australian High Court ordering a journalist to reveal sources so the subject could sue for defamation (1988). This judicial power can chill investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast licensing obligation to serve the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast licensors (e.g., FCC) issue licenses on the condition that broadcasters will 'serve the public interest'; licensing is a formal way the government controls broadcast content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasting differs from print because broadcast requires a license; the government asserts it licenses those 'it believes will serve the public interest.' Quoted critique: broadcasting treated as 'a ninth-class citizen' for First Amendment rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness Doctrine (requirement for opposing views)
rubrics_metrics.description: An FCC policy that required broadcasters to provide time for opposing views and to behave as 'fiduciaries' of the public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted in 1949 to protect public interests; critics argue its net effect chilled speech as broadcasters avoided controversy. The Doctrine was effectively repealed during deregulation in the 1980s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-time exemption for candidates in newscasts (1959 amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1959 congressional amendment exempted equal-time regulations for political candidates appearing in regular newscasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal carve-out separates paid political advertising rules from incidental/newscast appearances, affecting how candidate exposure is regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of deregulation on programming choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Deregulation (1980s onwards) reduced some regulatory constraints and had downstream effects on content: stations dropped or did not start news shows; tabloid TV formats proliferated; diversity did not necessarily increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some stations dropped news programs; tabloid shows lacking journalistic gatekeepers produced sensational content and occasionally tragic outcomes (Jenny Jones case). Deregulation removed broadcasters' obligation to account for programming/community service.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-trafficking rule (license-holding duration) and ownership turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule that required broadcast licensees to hold a license for at least three years before resale; repeal increased liquidity and led to rapid station turnover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeal turned broadcast properties into more liquid assets (115 stations sold <3 years between 1984–86 versus 10 in 1981–83). The 1992 Cable Act later included a provision against trafficking for cable system owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public television editorial rights (1984)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public TV stations were granted the right to editorialize (issue editorials), a formal policy change affecting public broadcast content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although given the right, lack of editorializing persisted—possibly due to 'journalistic timorousness.' This is a regulatory permission that may or may not change practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's programming regulation (Children's Television Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal restrictions specific to children's programming—the primary remaining broadcast restriction noted is the 1990 Children's Television Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deregulation otherwise removed many requirements for broadcasters to account for community service, creating favorable climate for advertiser-created children's shows whose primary purpose is to sell toys via show heroes (Kunkel, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use of secrecy, classification, and FoI procedures to control information
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative practices—reclassification of documents as secret, restrictive Freedom of Information (FoI) policies, and other secrecy routines—that limit journalists' access to government information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1980s–1990s examples: documents reclassified; Clinton administration review recommended presumption of public access but longstanding bureaucratic habits and rules (e.g., withholding electronic mail) continued to impede access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government effort to shape news via public information specialists and leaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Government employees and information specialists actively produce public information and use news leaks, backgrounders, and off-the-record interviews to set the news agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More than 3,000 U.S. government workers primarily produce public information designed to give impression of competence. Off-the-record briefings during Vietnam and other periods show how executives attempt to shape media framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military-controlled access and pool rules during conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria and ground rules imposed by the Department of Defense (DOD) for inclusion in National Media Pools and for reporters covering military operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed DOD 1992 criteria: familiarity with military coverage, maintain Washington bureau of sufficient size, be ready to deploy with equipment in four hours, agree to a set of ground rules (and mission-specific rules), and be owned/operated by U.S. companies. During the Gulf War, press pools, censorship of dispatches, and requirements to sign agreements limited independent coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military influence on media language and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The military's effective establishment of euphemistic or sanitized language ('knocked down', 'taken out', 'neutralized') that shapes how journalists describe combat and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of 'soft words' for 'hard combat' shows how official language can normalize or obscure the realities of warfare, influencing public perception via media framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketplace competition assumption: competition fosters diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonly held assumption that market competition (multiple newspapers or broadcasters) creates a 'marketplace of ideas' and thereby increases diversity in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies present mixed findings: some show little difference between competing newspapers; television may produce uniqueness as stations position themselves, but cable expansion has not necessarily increased substantive diversity because many channels draw from a few distributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local market structure effect on news and design
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of local competitors and relative circulation size affects editorial choices and design—smaller papers may modernize design when competing with larger rivals; suburban papers may increase local coverage when challenged by metropolitan encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies: Weaver & Mullins found little editorial difference with competition; Utt & Pasternack found smaller papers tended to be more modern in graphic design; Lacy suggests intercity competition can increase local news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global competition and emergence of international news markets (CNN effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The founding and ascendancy of global news services (e.g., CNN) created a global market for news and shifted expectations for international coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNN's rise (Tiananmen, fall of Berlin Wall, Persian Gulf War) made it a primary international news source; competitors (BBC World Service Television, alliances with ABC) emerged to share footage and bureaus, affecting how international news is gathered and distributed.
